**What a delegated certificate proves:** the program ran the goal's checks, through the shell executor, in the department worktree, on the tree the external agent left, and recorded the run and the certificate in the department's own session. That is the whole claim. It proves nothing about how the tree was produced: for an out-of-process provider no model-visible history of the implementer lives in this log, the department's trajectory carries no steps, and `usage` is recorded only for a child this process published and whose own session log accounts for tokens. Because `implementer` is inside the digest, the same goals staffed two ways are two programs — which is what makes comparing them a comparison of certificates over trees rather than of transcripts.

## Integration and release

Once every goal is certified, the service adds the integration worktree at `<workspaceRoot>/<programId>/@integration` — a key no lower-kebab-case goal key can claim — from the base revision, records `program/integration { running }`, and takes each department branch in dependency order. A branch whose head is no longer the revision the ledger recorded for that department is refused: the integration records `failed` naming both revisions, because a branch that moved is not what the program certified. A branch the integration worktree already contains, which is what an interrupted integration leaves behind, is skipped rather than merged again; every other branch is merged with `git merge --no-ff`.

It then creates the integration session over that worktree with a standard authored from `integration.checks` followed by one `gate-<n>` check per entry of `integration.gates`, so the integration certificate covers the gates as well as the checks. The checks run before any model turn, so a clean merge that passes needs none; a merged head that does not pass is what the integration goal is for. The certificate records `program/integration { certified, mergedRevision }`, every goal moves to `merged`, and `program/end { released, mergedRevision }` follows. A merge that fails and a merged head that never passes both record `program/integration { failed, reason }` and end the program `failed`.

The integration session is confined for as long as it runs. When `readBarrier` is composed, the service registers `denyFor(session, <workspaceRoot>/<programId>)`: the barrier grants a session its own workspace beneath a denied ancestor, and every department worktree is a sibling of the integration's inside that root, so the one registration reaches every department worktree and nothing of the integration's own. Both closing records carry `denied` with what was registered, empty for a composition that has no barrier, and the registration is disposed when the integration ends. `isolation` stays `none`: what the denial is worth is what the composed executors enforce, which is what the certificate's isolation claim already states.

## Resume

`resume()` lists persisted sessions, loads every program session with a `program/start` and no `program/end`, and reconciles each goal from its department's own log and worktree rather than from the ledger: a department session that does not exist is `pending`, one whose worktree is gone is `failed` because the branch is the evidence its certificate cites, one whose log carries a certificate is `certified` with the branch head read from the worktree, one whose goal is blocked is `blocked`, and anything else is `running`. Every status the reconciliation discovered is recorded, together with a declaration for any goal the ledger never recorded at all, before `program/resume` states the counts. Departments that are still running are resumed in place through `ctx.agents.resume` and the goal domain's own resume; pending goals whose dependencies have certified are started. Because a department's session id is derived from the program id and the key, no key ever gets a second session.

An integration the ledger left `running` is taken back over rather than opened again. Its session id is derived from the program id, so a second `create` would be refused by persistence and the interrupted integration could never finish: when persistence already holds that session, the pass resumes it through `ctx.agents.resume`, resumes its goal, and continues at the attempt after the validation runs its own log records, so the round cap covers the whole integration rather than each process. The standing `running` record is what this pass owns — no second one is appended, which the ledger's own transitions do not admit either — and a session that carries no goal to resume records `failed` with that reason. A `running` record whose process died before the session existed simply opens it, still under the one record.

A delegated department's `program/delegation` records are part of that log, and the highest attempt they carry is what the resumed pass continues after, so an attempt that already ended is never run a second time. The invariant companion holds the same relation for every department session: a `program/delegation` follows the session's `program/member` for the same key and carries an attempt strictly greater than every attempt already recorded there.

A program's optional `spec.tokenCeiling` is folded from the usage of every session carrying its `program/member` stamp, at each department start. A program that has spent its ceiling starts no further department, records the goals that never started `abandoned`, and ends `abandoned`.
